newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian upgrade possible in 1-3 years - S&P.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian upgrade possible in 1-3 years - S&P.

text.p: Australia's credit rating could be upgraded in the next one to three years if the government maintains its policy stance of cutting the budget deficit, the head of sovereign ratings for ratings agency Standard and Poor's, David Beers, said in an interview aired on Sunday.

S&P affirmed Australia's debt ratings and upgraded the outlook to positive from stable the day after the goverment's August 20 budget for 1996/97 to June 30 which outlined a plan to turn an underlying budget deficit of A$10.3 billion as of June 1996 into a surplus of A$1 billion by June 1999.

"A positive outlook means that it is possible with an extra one to three years that Standard and Poor's will raise the Commonwealth's credit rating from its current AA," Beers said on the Nine Network's Busines Sunday programme.
Beers said it was important that the government stuck to its plan to improve national savings and reduce the high external debt levels in order for the credit rating to be upgraded.

"So our message is really to investors to say that we think that if the current policy stance is sustained, then we think Australia's credit standing can improve a bit over the next couple of years," he said.

Beers said S&P was aware of the possibility of Senate obstruction of some budget measures, but he said that based on past experience "we're pretty confident that this government will be able to get through the bulk of what it's aiming to do in terms of its fiscal policy intact."
While the Senate may block or get changes to certain measures, it was the overall picture rather than the specific components that most concerned S&P, Beers said.

"Well, the specific bottom line issue is the size of the budget deficit and the aim and objective of the government to bringing that back into balance, so that's what we're focusing on in the main," Beers said.

While some change in policies was expected, especially given Australia's three-year election cycle, the size of the debt burden meant it was important that consistent policies to reduce the debt were maintained, he said.

"We're pretty confident that the political consensus is broadly there for these types of polices to be pursued, but we'll watch them for a while and see how some of these practical issues ... pan out," Beers said.
